title: Product Personalization Fulfillment at Scale: Production Files, Proofing and Supplier Routing
summary: Product personalization fulfillment breaks at volume. Here’s how to automate print-ready files, proofing and supplier handoff.
body_markdown:
[Katie Lynch was editing every order by hand](https://www.customily.com/post/customers-success-story-katie-j-design-events-customily) . Her Brisbane studio, Katie J Design & Events, designs, prints and packs personalized party décor in-house, and customers kept sending names and text that needed fixing before anything could print. Even autocorrect caused problems. She hired staff to keep up, then realized that adding people wasn’t going to solve it.


That’s the wall most custom-product stores hit.[Product personalization fulfillment](https://www.customily.com/our-features#automatic-print-files) works fine at 20 orders a day and falls apart at 200, because every order needs its own artwork before it can be produced. This guide covers where that breaks (production files, proofing, and supplier handoff) and how to fix each one before you add volume.


### Why personalized orders break standard fulfillment


A standard print-on-demand order is simple: SKU in, product out. A personalized order carries extra baggage. It has customer-entered text, maybe an uploaded photo, a font choice, a color, and a product that needs all of that placed correctly on a specific print area.


Every one of those inputs is a chance for something to go wrong. A name with an apostrophe renders as a blank box. A phone photo is 800 pixels wide. A customer picks light text on a light product.


Most stores handle this in one of two ways. Either someone reviews every order manually, which works until it doesn’t scale, or nobody reviews anything and refunds absorb the errors. Neither is a plan. The goal is to automate the predictable majority and give a human only the exceptions.


### Print-ready file generation and proofing: where errors start


Let’s get specific about what “print-ready” means, because it’s the step people hand-wave.


A print-ready file has to match the production method and the supplier’s spec for that exact product: dimensions, resolution, bleed, safe area, color mode, and file format. A 15 oz mug and an 11 oz mug have different print areas. A phone case for one model has cutouts another doesn’t. Build the file against the wrong template and the supplier either rejects it or prints it wrong, and you often find out when the customer does.


Doing this by hand means one designer, one template library, and a very long queue. The alternative is generating the file automatically from the order data. The customer’s text, font, color and image get placed into the product template, the file is exported in the format production needs, and it travels with the order without anyone opening a design tool.


That’s what[Customily](https://www.customily.com/) does for every personalized order, and it’s what changed things for Katie. She pre-set her base files with the cut lines production needs, so each order comes out correctly sized and ready to print. For apparel, files go straight to her print-on-demand provider. In her words, the long-term fix was smarter tools, and she was able to reallocate two full-time team members who used to handle manual editing. Customer service tickets dropped too.


A few details matter once you’re past a few dozen orders a day:


- **It’s not just for DTG or sublimation.** Customily generates files for print, engraving, laser cutting and embroidery, so the same setup works whether you outsource or run your own equipment.
- **Formats cover most production workflows.** You can download PDF, AI, PNG, JPG, EPS, DXF, OFM and more, depending on what your machine or supplier wants.
- **Multi-location products are handled in one order.** Front and back of a t-shirt, or each item in a bundle, can each get their own design.
- **File names carry order details.** When you’re processing hundreds of files, a name that includes the order information saves you from opening each one to figure out what it is.
- **Bulk download.** Pull all print files at once instead of grabbing them one by one.


None of that is glamorous. It’s the stuff that decides whether your Tuesday morning takes twenty minutes or three hours.


#### Proofing: catch problems before production, not after


Proofing sounds like one step, but it happens in two places, and you want both.


**Before purchase.** A live preview lets the buyer see their text or photo on the actual product before they pay. That cuts “I didn’t realize it would look like that” tickets, because the customer has already approved what they’re getting. It’s the cheapest proofing you’ll ever do, since the customer does it for you. Katie’s customers now edit and preview their products in real time, which is a big part of why the back-and-forth over text placement went away.


**After purchase.** Even with a preview, you want a place to review an order before it goes to production. In **Customily** you can open an order’s details and edit the print file if something needs correcting, then send it on. That matters most for the odd cases: a long name that wraps badly, a photo that needs repositioning, a customer who emails after checkout to change a spelling.


What should you check on orders that get a second look? A few things cause most problems:


- Uploaded images with low resolution
- Text that overflows its area or shrinks to unreadable size
- Characters the chosen font can’t render
- Low contrast between the design and the product color


My opinion: reviewing every order by hand is a trap. It feels safe, but it caps your growth at however many orders your reviewer can eyeball per day, and tired reviewers miss things anyway. Set the product options up so the common mistakes can’t happen (font limits, character limits, sensible print areas), then spend human attention on the exceptions.


### Order routing and supplier handoff: getting each order to the right place


Once the file is right, it has to go somewhere. With one supplier that’s trivial. Once you add a second or third, routing becomes its own problem. If you’ve searched for Shopify order routing rules, this is the pain behind that query: personalized orders need the right file going to the right producer.


Common reasons to use multiple suppliers:


- Different products need different producers (apparel, drinkware and wall art rarely come from the same place)
- You want a domestic option for faster shipping and an overseas one for lower cost
- You need a backup when your main supplier hits capacity, especially in Q4


When you decide where an order goes, the inputs worth thinking about are product type, destination, cost or margin, and supplier availability. Product type is the easy one and the one to set up first.


Two things trip people up. First, an order with multiple items can split across suppliers, which means multiple shipments and multiple tracking numbers, so your customer notifications have to cope. Second, each supplier has its own file spec, so the file and the destination can’t be decided separately. A file built for Supplier A’s template is useless sent to Supplier B.


On the **Customily** side, you have two paths. You can send orders directly to[connected POD partners](https://www.customily.com/print-on-demand) , or export a CSV and fulfill with whoever you like. Customily can also connect with any printing system, so a supplier that isn’t in the partner network isn’t a dead end. Either way, you track and manage orders from one place instead of juggling dashboards, with real-time updates on where each one stands.


### How to scale a print on demand business without scaling errors


If you’re trying to figure out how to scale a print on demand business, the pattern is consistent: volume exposes whatever’s manual. The order you fix things in matters.


1. **Standardize templates first.** One clean, correct template per product beats a folder of near-duplicates.
2. **Automate file generation.** This is the biggest time sink and the biggest source of errors.
3. **Tighten your product options.** Limit fonts, set character limits, define print areas, so bad inputs never get through.
4. **Roll out in stages.** Katie connected her catalog one product at a time over about two years, starting with her top 25 themes. She also trained customers on the new system gradually instead of switching everything at once. You don’t need to be that slow, but the principle holds: prove it on your best sellers first.
5. **Then add suppliers.** More suppliers on a shaky process just multiply the problems.
6. **Centralize order tracking.** One view of every order’s status beats a spreadsheet and five tabs.


Resist the urge to start with the supplier side because it looks like the “scaling” part. Sending a bad file to a faster supplier just delivers the mistake sooner.


### What to look for in a personalization fulfillment setup


Whatever stack you use, check these before you commit:


- Does it generate production files automatically from the order, or does it just collect the data and leave the file to you?
- Does it output the formats your production method needs?
- Can it handle multiple print locations and bundles?
- Does it connect to the suppliers or systems you already use?
- What happens when something goes wrong? Is there a person you can reach?


That last one matters more than it sounds. When a batch of orders goes sideways at 9 p.m. during peak season, a help center article won’t save you. **Customily’s support is live chat** with real people, not bots, with coverage across US and Pacific time zones almost around the clock. There’s also one-on-one training and weekly live classes, so your team isn’t learning the setup on a deadline. Katie named the support team as one of the reasons she committed.


### Wrapping up


Fulfillment at scale comes down to removing the manual steps that don’t need a human: building files, standardizing inputs, and getting orders to the right place. Keep people for the exceptions and for customer problems that need judgment.

### Frequently Asked Questions


**What is personalization in fulfillment?**


It’s the part of order fulfillment that deals with customer-specific details: turning a buyer’s text, photo, or design choices into a production-ready file and getting it to the right supplier. Standard fulfillment moves a fixed product. Personalized fulfillment has to build the product’s artwork for each order first.


**How do you fulfill custom orders without manual file prep?**


Use software that generates the print file automatically from the order data and delivers it in the format your production method needs. With Customily, each personalized order gets its file generated for you, and you can download files in bulk or send them to a POD partner.


**Can you use more than one supplier for personalized products?**


Yes, and many sellers do. You need to match each product’s file to the right supplier’s specs and plan for split shipments with multiple tracking numbers. Customily lets you send orders to POD partners or export a CSV to fulfill with any supplier.


**When should I add suppliers to a personalized product business?**


After your files and templates are reliable. Adding suppliers earlier just sends flawed files to more places. Fix file generation and product options first, then expand your supplier mix.
